h1: The 6 Best Video Doorbells for Apartments, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 video doorbells for apartments, scored on battery or wired power, video resolution, subscription needs and renter setup.
summary: The BOIFUN 2K wireless doorbell is the best fit for most apartment renters: a battery model that needs no wiring and carries no subscription. The Tapo 2K adds a chime for similar money, and the aosu 5MP works either wired or wireless. The Blink is the lightweight Amazon-ecosystem pick, while the Aqara G400 suits only units with an Ethernet run at the door.
intro: Apartment renters shop for video doorbells with a constraint homeowners don't have: you can't rewire anything, and drilling into the door frame can cost a deposit. That makes power the first decision, not resolution. A wired model that needs 16 to 24 volts from a doorbell transformer is a non-starter if your building has none, and a battery model is the only choice that installs in an afternoon.

We ranked six doorbells by how well they suit a renter: battery or wireless power, video quality, subscription requirements and ease of removal when you move out. Several are cheap enough to treat as disposable, which is a feature when you rent. One pick needs Ethernet and a PoE source, which most apartments lack, and we ranked it accordingly.

products.name: BOIFUN Video Doorbell Camera Wireless - No Subscription Required
products.verdict: A 2K battery doorbell with no wiring and no required subscription.
products.description:
The BOIFUN is a 2K wireless video doorbell running on a battery, sold with no subscription required, in the $25 to $50 tier.

Those three facts add up to a renter's doorbell. Battery power means no landlord-approved wiring, 2K resolution gives a clearer face than 1080p HD models like the Blink, and the lack of a mandatory plan means the camera keeps working without a monthly bill. It ranks first because it is the cheapest of the strong options. The tradeoff of any battery doorbell is recharging, so expect to pull it down every few months.

Buy it if you rent and want an easy, subscription-free camera. The caveat: check what local storage it offers, since without a cloud plan you rely on that.
products.idealFor: Renters who want a cheap, easy camera with no monthly bill.

products.name: Tapo 2K Wireless Smart Video Doorbell w/Chime
products.verdict: A 2K battery doorbell that includes a chime for the inside of the apartment.
products.description:
The Tapo is a 2K wireless doorbell running on a battery, sold with a chime, in the $25 to $50 tier.

The chime is the practical advantage. Many battery doorbells ring only on your phone, which fails the moment you leave it in another room, and a plug-in chime gives a physical sound. It matches the BOIFUN on 2K resolution and price tier, and trails it only by requiring you to check whether the chime and cloud features fit your habits. Tapo is a smart-home brand with a broader range of devices.

Buy it if you want an audible ring in the apartment without wiring. The caveat is that the chime needs an outlet, and you should check the storage options before you buy.
products.idealFor: Renters who want an audible ring, not just a phone alert.
products.skipIf: You never miss notifications and want the simplest setup.

products.name: aosu 5MP Ultra HD Wireless & Wired Video Doorbell Camera
products.verdict: A 5MP camera that runs on battery or wired power, depending on your door.
products.description:
The aosu is a 5MP doorbell that works either wireless on battery or wired, sitting in the $100 to $200 tier, the highest here except the Aqara's wiring needs.

Flexibility is why it makes the list. If your building has doorbell wiring and the landlord allows it, you can wire it and never charge a battery. If not, you can run it wireless. Its 5MP sensor is the highest resolution on this list. It ranks third because the price tier is much higher than the BOIFUN and Tapo, and it offers no feature that clearly justifies the premium.

Buy it if you might move to a place with different wiring. The caveat: a high price for a renter's device.
products.idealFor: Renters who move often between homes with different wiring.

products.name: Blink Video Doorbell - Head-to-toe HD view
products.verdict: A head-to-toe HD doorbell that runs on battery or wired power.
products.description:
The Blink doorbell offers an HD head-to-toe view, can be wired or run on battery, and sits in the $25 to $50 tier.

The head-to-toe view means a tall frame, so you see a package on the doormat as well as a visitor's face. HD is a step below the 2K on the BOIFUN and Tapo, which is why it ranks fourth, but it comes from a known brand within an Amazon ecosystem, which matters if you already use that app. The battery option works for renters, and wiring is available if allowed.

Buy it if you already own Blink or Alexa devices and want one app. The caveat: HD is lower resolution than 2K rivals at the same price.
products.idealFor: Renters already using Blink or Alexa devices.
products.skipIf: You want the sharpest video at this price.

products.name: BOIFUN Video Doorbell Camera Wireless
products.verdict: Another 2K battery BOIFUN, with less explicit subscription wording.
products.description:
This second BOIFUN is a 2K wireless battery doorbell in the $25 to $50 tier, without the no-subscription label in its title.

The hardware class matches the top BOIFUN, so the difference is mostly in what the listing promises. It does not state that no subscription is required, so you need to confirm that before buying. It ranks fifth because the top listing makes the commitment clear, and the Tapo adds a chime. As a pure battery 2K camera, it still suits an apartment.

Buy it if it is cheaper at the time or the other listing is out of stock. The caveat: check subscription terms first.
products.idealFor: Renters who find this listing cheaper than the main BOIFUN.
products.skipIf: You want a clear no-subscription promise.

products.name: Aqara Doorbell Camera G400 with Chime
products.verdict: A wired Power-over-Ethernet doorbell with a chime, for doors with a cable run.
products.description:
The Aqara G400 is a wired Power-over-Ethernet doorbell with a chime, in the $50 to $100 tier.

PoE sends power and data over one cable, which gives reliable video and no batteries. The problem for renters is that few apartment doors have an Ethernet cable behind them, so installation usually needs a landlord and a cable run. It ranks last for that reason. If your building does provide a network drop at the door, it becomes a strong choice.

Buy it if your unit already has Ethernet at the door or you own the wall. The caveat: for most renters, a battery model is the practical answer.
products.idealFor: Units with a network cable at the door.
products.skipIf: You can't run a cable or change the wiring.

methodology.description: 5MP and 2K ranked above HD, since a clearer image is the point of a doorbell camera.

methodology.title: Subscription requirements
methodology.description: A stated no-subscription promise scored higher than listings that left the terms unclear.

methodology.title: Indoor alert
methodology.description: A chime or similar indoor sounder counted, because phone-only alerts fail when the phone is out of reach.

methodology.description: Lower-cost units ranked higher since they are easier to remove or replace when you move.

whatMatters.detail: Battery doorbells need no wiring and install in minutes, but you must recharge them every few months. Wired models run continuously but need doorbell wiring or Ethernet. For renters, battery is usually the practical choice. Check the listing for the power type and whether a plug-in option exists.

Resolution decides whether you can read a face or a package label. HD is 1080p, 2K is sharper, and 5MP sharper still. Look for the figure in the title, and note that field of view matters as much, since a wide view like the Blink's head-to-toe shows packages on the floor.

Many cameras save clips only if you pay a monthly plan. Some, like the BOIFUN, state no subscription is required. Look for how recordings are stored and whether live view is free, because a cheap camera with a required plan costs more across a year.

A doorbell that only notifies a phone can be missed. A plug-in chime, as on the Tapo and Aqara, rings in the apartment. Check whether a chime is included, and whether it plugs into an outlet or needs separate wiring.

Renters need a mount that leaves little damage. Screws, adhesive and door-mounted brackets differ. Check how the doorbell attaches and whether your lease allows it, and ask whether the building has its own entry system that you should not cover.

faq.q: Can I install a video doorbell in an apartment?
faq.a: Usually, if your lease allows it and the building has no shared entry camera policy. A battery model such as the BOIFUN or Tapo needs no wiring, but check with your landlord about mounting.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake apartment renters make here?
faq.a: Buying a wired model without checking the door. The Aqara G400 needs Ethernet and the wired aosu mode needs doorbell wiring. Most renters are better served by a battery model.

faq.q: Is the Tapo worth it over the BOIFUN?
faq.a: If you want an indoor ring, yes. The Tapo includes a chime, while the BOIFUN no-subscription model relies on phone alerts. Both are 2K battery doorbells in the same $25 to $50 tier.

faq.q: How do I set up a battery doorbell?
faq.a: Charge the battery, connect the doorbell to your Wi-Fi in the app, then mount it with the supplied bracket. Test the signal at the door first, since a weak signal causes missed alerts.

faq.q: How often do I recharge the battery?
faq.a: Every few months, depending on traffic at your door. A busy hallway drains faster. The Blink and aosu can be wired to avoid recharging if your building allows it.
The BOIFUN no-subscription model says it does not. For the Tapo, Blink and aosu, check the listing for what recording and cloud features cost, and confirm that live view stays free.

finalTake: The BOIFUN 2K no-subscription doorbell is the best fit for apartments: it runs on a battery, needs no wiring and avoids monthly fees. The Tapo is the better choice when you want an indoor chime, and the aosu 5MP suits renters who move between wired and unwired doors. Skip the Aqara G400 unless your door already has Ethernet.
